project.name: Q088 · How can we develop manufacturing systems on Mars?
project.question:
It is not too far-fetched to presume that one day human beings will leave Earth and emigrate to Mars. A stunning red orb with mountains and valleys not unlike those on our world, Mars is the planet in our solar system that is most similar to Earth. Exploratory missions, including China’s first Mars mission, Tianwen-1, which is currently in orbit, aim to reveal information that will be vital should we ever establish colonies there. But to take this step, we will need to develop functional and economically viable manufacturing systems that can operate in the unique ecosystem and climate limitations of Mars.

The extreme environments of Mars challenge existing manufacturing theories and methods. Scientists and engineers must consider the many elements that would impact effective production there, including extreme temperature, solar radiation, and microgravity. We must also contend with questions about fuel and energy to power manufacturing and habitats on the Red

Planet. This interdisciplinary quest requires scientists and engineers from seemingly disparate fields to collaborate across the globe.

One key to Mars manufacturing will be utilizing the resources the planet has to offer. This is especially pertinent given the distance between Earth and Mars (225 million kilometers) and the prohibitive cost of shipping materials through space. Martian geology is a potential gold mine: Its regolith—a layer of loose, rocky material located on the planet’s surface—could be very useful as a prime construction material, once we develop the technical capabilities to bind it and build with it.

3D printing may be a game-changing technology in this respect, especially as we continue to advance our expertise in materials science, engineering, and chemistry, combined with the software and hardware innovations necessary for large-scale 3D printing.

payload.title: Regolith Construction Trade Study
payload.rationale: Compare processing routes under energy, mass, strength, and maintenance constraints to identify viable pathways for in-situ resource utilization.
payload.completion_test: A requirements matrix and bounded candidate comparison that authorizes selection of a baseline architecture for prototyping.

brief.title: Regolith Construction Trade Study: Conceptual Feasibility & Evidence Gap Assessment
learned: In-situ resource utilization is essential for reducing mission costs and transport burdens for off-world colonization.
Shape-optimized geometries that prioritize compressive stress over tensile stress offer theoretical pathways for significant material and energy savings.
Current literature predominantly covers conceptual designs and lunar analogs, lacking direct empirical validation for Martian environmental conditions.
Critical source extraction failures disrupted the analytical pipeline for Martian habitat and autonomous robotics data.
evidence: Supports the conceptual rationale for transitioning from Earth-prefabricated modules to localized regolith-based architectures.
Validates environmental stressors including vacuum pressure differentials, extreme thermal cycling, ionizing radiation, and abrasive dust degradation.
Demonstrates algorithmic geometric optimization can theoretically reduce construction mass and energy by over 50% compared to conventional precast or inflatable designs.
Provides only abstract-level comparisons and introductory context rather than quantitative performance benchmarks.
limitations: Cannot authorize a baseline architecture or satisfy the completion test requirement for a requirements matrix and bounded candidate comparison.
Fails to account for Martian regolith heterogeneity, binder/water scarcity, and multi-axial loading, rendering efficiency claims speculative.
Lacks empirical data on polymer outgassing, seal degradation, autonomous deployment logistics, and long-term operational durability.
Scope misalignment between lunar experimental contexts and Mars mission objectives prevents direct application of findings.
open_questions: How do site-specific Martian regolith compositions and chemical binders impact compressive strength and long-term structural integrity?
What are the quantified energy, mass, and maintenance trade-offs across competing ISRU processing routes under simulated Martian conditions?
Can autonomous placement and large-scale additive manufacturing systems operate reliably within constrained power and mass budgets?
Which structural forms best balance fabrication complexity, deployment logistics, and resilience against micrometeorite impacts and thermal fatigue?
next_moves: Resolve upstream extraction failures and acquire valid technical reports on Martian habitat construction and autonomous swarm logistics.
Develop a standardized requirements matrix and bounded candidate comparison through targeted literature synthesis to enable structured trade-off analysis.
Conduct site-specific regolith characterization and multi-physics stress modeling to ground theoretical efficiency claims in empirical data.
Execute accelerated aging, vacuum-dust abrasion, and full-scale additive manufacturing trials under simulated Martian conditions before architectural selection.
Temporarily scale the direction scope to a conceptual feasibility review while quantitative validation pipelines and prototyping tests are established.

findings.recommendation: Resolve upstream extraction failures for Martian habitat and robotics sources. Align cited literature with the Mars-focused remaining work, or adjust the direction scope to match the available lunar-centric evidence.

Scale back the immediate trade study scope to a conceptual feasibility review until quantitative data on processing routes, energy/mass budgets, and structural testing are obtained. Supplement with peer-reviewed engineering studies containing empirical trade-off matrices.

Reconstruct the analytical pipeline by retrieving valid text for the Martian habitat and autonomous swarm sources. Bridge the gap between environmental constraints and processing route selection with intermediate technical reports or simulation data.

Generate the required requirements matrix and bounded candidate comparison internally or through targeted literature synthesis before proceeding. The current evidence lacks the structured evaluation criteria and performance benchmarks needed to authorize a baseline architecture.

review.summary: Scientific validity and inference scope are critically compromised. The evidentiary base consists primarily of introductory contexts and abstract-level conceptual proposals, failing to provide the quantitative processing route data, structural metrics, or trade study matrices mandated by the completion test. Two cited sources suffer from extraction failures, breaking the analytical chain. Consequently, the direction cannot be admitted without repairing these gaps, aligning the lunar/Mars focus, and supplying detailed engineering analysis and structured evaluation artifacts.

Multiscale experimental testing - Previous article in this issue - Next article in this issue ## Introduction The aspiration to construct lunar habitats and
achieve long-term residency has always fueled humanity's drive. As the closest celestial body to Earth and the gateway to deep space exploration for humans, the
moon holds significant material, environmental, and positional resources. Establishing permanent lunar habitats is an inevitable choice for lunar scientific
research, resource development, and maintaining space peace and stability. In 2019, the United States introduced the Artemis Program, aiming to establish a
sustainable presence on the lunar surface within the next decade [1]. In 2021, China and Russia unveiled their plan to construct the International Lunar
Research Station (ILRS), focusing on creating scientific research facilities in the lunar polar regions [2,3]. Additionally, Europe, Japan, South Korea, and
India have also announced their intentions for lunar exploration [[4], [5], [6], [7]]. Consequently, the construction of lunar habitats has emerged as a crucial
engineering requirement and technical challenge in lunar exploration missions. Lunar construction poses formidable challenges, primarily in transporting
materials from the Earth to the moon. This endeavor demands substantial resources, including finances, energy, time, and effort. Other harsh conditions,
characterized by limited energy supplies, the lack of mechanical equipment, and the absence of human assistance, compound the complexity of lunar construction.
Moreover, the extreme lunar environments introduce unique structural loading considerations. The vacuum environment induces substantial pressure differences in
internal and external environments, imposing significant tensile loads on structures. This is a common issue in space structures. Furthermore, lunar temperature
variation far exceeds that experienced on the Earth, exposing structures to considerable thermal stresses. In addition, lunar structures must cope with

weathering and solar wind. Furthermore, although rare, micrometeorites and moonquakes introduce potential threats to structures. Micrometeorite impact may cause

## Sustainable colonization of Mars using shape optimized structures and in situ concrete | Scientific Reports

**Source**: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-023-42971-9

---

[Skip to main content](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-023-42971-9?error=cookies_not_supported&code=71d0083f-8ad0-4518-8c53-0b031fa959f4#content)

and JavaScript.

Sustainable colonization of Mars using shape optimized structures and in situ concrete

[Download PDF](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-023-42971-9.pdf)

[Download PDF](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-023-42971-9.pdf)

## Abstract

The major obstacle to Martian colonization is the mission cost which requires significant reduction. From the structural engineering point of view, importing
materials and structural elements from Earth or massive excavations on the surface of Mars require an enormous amount of energy; thus, inflatable and under-
surface structures as the main options for Martian colonization seem unrealistically expensive. Construction of affordable buildings onsite using only in situ
sources may represent an ideal solution for Martian colonization. On the other hand, solar energy, at the early stage of colonization, would be the only
available, practical, and low-cost energy source on Mars. Though, for sustainable and broad colonization, the energy required for construction and the
construction cost should be minimized. Here, we propose three types of simple (relatively optimized), perforated, and algorithmic shape-optimized Martian
structures to minimize the material and energy required for construction as well as the construction cost using only in situ resources. These structural forms
can be considered remarkable steps towards sustainable structural construction and colonization on Mars. Also, these innovative structures were designed to
minimize the tensile stress (maximize the compressive stress) and enable the use of in situ concrete. Our data indicate that compared to our previous study, the
material and energy required for construction as well as the construction cost can be reduced by more than 50%. Acceptance criteria and limitations appropriate
to the Martian environment, and desirable structural and material behaviors were defined to evaluate whether or not the behavior of a structure under the
applied loads and conditions will be acceptable. To detect potential issues for onsite construction and evaluate the geometry of the models, a 1:200 3D model of
the best structural form was printed.

- [Civil engineering](https://www.nature.com/subjects/civil-engineering)

## Introduction

Earth has experienced five massive extinction events where almost 85% of living species have become extinct in the past 500 million
years[1](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-023-42971-9#ref-CR1). Some scholars assert that we are now in the midst of the Holocene massive extinction where
the increase in the human population and unchecked devastation of its resources will go beyond Earth’s carrying capacity to rejuvenate itself. Some scientists
believe that human beings will be forced to seek out energy supplies from other sources such as planets and
stars[2](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-023-42971-9?error=cookies_not_supported&code=71d0083f-8ad0-4518-8c53-0b031fa959f4#ref-
CR2),[3](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-023-42971-9?error=cookies_not_supported&code=71d0083f-8ad0-4518-8c53-0b031fa959f4#ref-
CR3),[4](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-023-42971-9#ref-CR4). A multi-planetary life could be an appropriate answer to such concerns. Additionally, it
could provide economic opportunities such as space tourism, new resources to exploit, exploration of new worlds and help humanity to reach its full
potential[5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-023-42971-9#ref-CR5),[6](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-023-42971-9#ref-CR6). Thus, multi-planetary
life seems inevitable and Mars will most likely be our first destination.

With the increase in knowledge and data about Mars and its behavior, studies focusing on the colonization and construction on Mars have accelerated in the
present century[7](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-023-42971-9#ref-CR7). The Lunar/Mars Program Office at Johnson Space Center proposed a precast
prestressed concrete structure with a diameter of 36 m and height of 22 m (dome-shaped) which tolerated the desired internal pressure for planetary
use[8](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-023-42971-9#ref-CR8). NASA studied suitable structural forms for human settlements on Mars for a total mission
time of 919 days (224 days outbound from Earth, 458 days on Mars and 237 days of inbound to Earth)[9](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-023-42971-9#ref-
CR9). The structure was metal and cylindrical in shape with a diameter of 8 m that could tolerate the internal pressure difference. On such a mission, more than
20% of the mission cost would be for the structures/habitats to be imported from Earth.

Inflatable structures are among the most interesting types of structures proposed for life on Mars. These would be relatively lighter than steel structures and
easy to pack and deploy. One of the best examples of inflatable structures is TransHab[10](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-023-42971-9#ref-CR10).

The use of caves and glass domes as human habitats also have been studied. Caves are good for load bearing and could be sealed; however, their availability,
size and conditions on Mars have not been ascertained. They may be a good option for the second stage of
colonization[11](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-023-42971-9#ref-CR11).

direction.title: Regolith Construction Trade Study
direction.rationale: Compare processing routes under energy, mass, strength, and maintenance constraints to identify viable pathways for in-situ resource utilization.
direction.completion_test: A requirements matrix and bounded candidate comparison that authorizes selection of a baseline architecture for prototyping.
direction.remaining: Mars material tests and prototypes to validate structural performance and scalability.

claims.text: Shape-optimized Martian habitat structures utilizing in-situ concrete can achieve greater than 50% reduction in material and energy requirements compared to conventional precast or inflatable designs, contingent upon maintaining compressive stress dominance under Martian environmental loads.
claims.scope: Conceptual design and comparative analysis of Martian colonization habitats

rebuttal.challenge: The >50% resource reduction metric is derived from algorithmic geometric optimization that ignores Martian regolith heterogeneity, binder/water scarcity, and multi-axial loading. Assuming compressive stress dominance overlooks tensile and shear failures from thermal fatigue, micrometeorite impacts, and abrasive dust degradation, which could rapidly compromise structural margins.
rebuttal.repair: Ground the efficiency claim in site-specific regolith characterization data, integrate multi-physics stress modeling (tensile, shear, cyclic fatigue), and validate with full-scale additive manufacturing trials under simulated Martian environmental conditions before authorizing architectural selection.

claims.text: Lunar construction methodologies will transition from heavy Earth-prefabricated modules to localized regolith bag architectures once multiscale experimental testing confirms structural viability against vacuum pressure differentials and extreme thermal cycles.
claims.scope: Early-stage lunar surface infrastructure planning and material selection

rebuttal.challenge: The transition hypothesis presumes regolith bag architectures will maintain integrity under prolonged vacuum exposure, ionizing radiation, and electrostatically charged abrasive dust without empirical validation. Cited multiscale testing lacks data on polymer outgassing, seal degradation, and autonomous placement logistics, leaving the structural viability assumption speculative.
rebuttal.repair: Execute accelerated aging and vacuum-dust abrasion tests on candidate bag composites, paired with autonomous deployment simulations to quantify placement mass/energy budgets, thereby replacing conceptual transition assumptions with empirically verified deployment readiness metrics.

claims.text: Current feasibility assessments for off-world in-situ construction remain bounded by the exclusion of full-scale structural simulations, detailed construction methodologies, and long-term operational performance data, limiting definitive architectural authorization to abstract-level conceptual comparisons.
claims.scope: Engineering trade studies and baseline architecture selection for extraterrestrial habitats

rebuttal.challenge: Although accurately noting the evidentiary gap, this bound statement offers no mechanism to bridge conceptual analysis to actionable engineering decisions. Without a standardized requirements matrix, abstract comparisons cannot resolve competing processing routes because energy, mass, strength, and maintenance trade-offs remain unquantified and unweighted against mission constraints.

findings.recommendation: Replace introductory and abstract-level citations with peer-reviewed engineering studies containing empirical trade-off matrices and quantitative performance data to substantiate the proposed efficiency and transition claims.

Scale back the immediate trade study scope to a conceptual feasibility review until quantitative data on processing routes, energy/mass budgets, and structural testing are obtained, ensuring the analytical boundaries match the available evidence.

Resolve upstream extraction failures for Martian habitat and autonomous swarm sources, or substitute them with accessible technical reports to bridge the analytical gap between environmental constraints and processing route selection.

Generate the required requirements matrix and bounded candidate comparison internally or through targeted literature synthesis before proceeding, as current evidence lacks the structured evaluation criteria and performance benchmarks needed to authorize a baseline architecture.

review.summary: Scientific validity and inference scope are critically compromised. The evidentiary base consists primarily of introductory contexts and abstract-level conceptual proposals, failing to provide the quantitative processing route data, structural metrics, or trade study matrices mandated by the completion test. Two cited sources suffer from extraction failures, breaking the analytical chain. Consequently, the direction cannot be admitted without repairing these gaps, aligning the lunar/Mars focus, and supplying detailed engineering analysis and structured evaluation artifacts.

output.title: Regolith Construction Trade Study: Conceptual Feasibility & Evidence Gap Assessment
learned: In-situ resource utilization is essential for reducing mission costs and transport burdens for off-world colonization.
Shape-optimized geometries that prioritize compressive stress over tensile stress offer theoretical pathways for significant material and energy savings.
Current literature predominantly covers conceptual designs and lunar analogs, lacking direct empirical validation for Martian environmental conditions.
Critical source extraction failures disrupted the analytical pipeline for Martian habitat and autonomous robotics data.
evidence: Supports the conceptual rationale for transitioning from Earth-prefabricated modules to localized regolith-based architectures.
Validates environmental stressors including vacuum pressure differentials, extreme thermal cycling, ionizing radiation, and abrasive dust degradation.
Demonstrates algorithmic geometric optimization can theoretically reduce construction mass and energy by over 50% compared to conventional precast or inflatable designs.
Provides only abstract-level comparisons and introductory context rather than quantitative performance benchmarks.
limitations: Cannot authorize a baseline architecture or satisfy the completion test requirement for a requirements matrix and bounded candidate comparison.
Fails to account for Martian regolith heterogeneity, binder/water scarcity, and multi-axial loading, rendering efficiency claims speculative.
Lacks empirical data on polymer outgassing, seal degradation, autonomous deployment logistics, and long-term operational durability.
Scope misalignment between lunar experimental contexts and Mars mission objectives prevents direct application of findings.
open_questions: How do site-specific Martian regolith compositions and chemical binders impact compressive strength and long-term structural integrity?
What are the quantified energy, mass, and maintenance trade-offs across competing ISRU processing routes under simulated Martian conditions?
Can autonomous placement and large-scale additive manufacturing systems operate reliably within constrained power and mass budgets?
Which structural forms best balance fabrication complexity, deployment logistics, and resilience against micrometeorite impacts and thermal fatigue?
next_moves: Resolve upstream extraction failures and acquire valid technical reports on Martian habitat construction and autonomous swarm logistics.
Develop a standardized requirements matrix and bounded candidate comparison through targeted literature synthesis to enable structured trade-off analysis.
Conduct site-specific regolith characterization and multi-physics stress modeling to ground theoretical efficiency claims in empirical data.
Execute accelerated aging, vacuum-dust abrasion, and full-scale additive manufacturing trials under simulated Martian conditions before architectural selection.
Temporarily scale the direction scope to a conceptual feasibility review while quantitative validation pipelines and prototyping tests are established.

findings.recommendation: Resolve upstream extraction failures for Martian habitat and robotics sources. Align cited literature with the Mars-focused remaining work, or adjust the direction scope to match the available lunar-centric evidence.

Scale back the immediate trade study scope to a conceptual feasibility review until quantitative data on processing routes, energy/mass budgets, and structural testing are obtained. Supplement with peer-reviewed engineering studies containing empirical trade-off matrices.

Reconstruct the analytical pipeline by retrieving valid text for the Martian habitat and autonomous swarm sources. Bridge the gap between environmental constraints and processing route selection with intermediate technical reports or simulation data.

Generate the required requirements matrix and bounded candidate comparison internally or through targeted literature synthesis before proceeding. The current evidence lacks the structured evaluation criteria and performance benchmarks needed to authorize a baseline architecture.
